2027-06-09.title: Wednesday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Ephrem, Deacon and Doctor of the Church
readings: not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life
Holy is the Lord our God
I have come not to abolish but to fulfill
2027-06-09.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Ephrem, deacon and doctor of the Church, may be kept today. He is dear to the Syriac Churches of Kerala as Mar Aprem, and the Syro-Malabar Church keeps his feast today too. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-06-09.verse: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
theo: In the Second Letter to the Corinthians Paul has to defend his ministry against people who came to Corinth with impressive letters of recommendation. He answers: I need no letters; “You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts,” “written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” Today's reading continues: “Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” Paul is thinking of Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, when God would write his law on the heart, and of Ezekiel's promise of a new spirit. He compares the giving of the Law on Sinai, which came “in glory so that the people of Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of the glory of his face,” with the ministry of the Spirit, and concludes: “how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?” We must read this carefully. Paul, a Jew who loved the Law, does not say the Law was bad. Elsewhere he writes: “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). He means that a law written outside us, on stone, can show us what is right but cannot give us the power to do it; it can only condemn the one who fails. The Spirit writes God's will within us and gives life. The glory of Sinai was real; the glory of the Spirit is greater and lasting. The Psalm sings the holiness of the God who spoke to Moses and Aaron and Samuel “in the pillar of cloud” and was “a forgiving God to them.”

The Gospel guards us against a wrong conclusion. If the Spirit gives life and the letter kills, should Christians throw away the commandments? Jesus answers clearly: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.” He respects even the smallest marks of the Scripture: “not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.” The Ten Commandments still stand; Jesus will show in the coming days that he asks for more, not less: not only no murder, but no anger; not only no adultery, but a pure heart. Fulfilment means bringing the Law to its full meaning, as a flower fulfils the bud. Jesus fulfils the Law by living it perfectly, by revealing its heart, which is love, and by giving the Spirit who makes us able to keep it. St Ephrem the Syrian, whom we may remember today, was born around 306 in Nisibis, served the Church there as a deacon and teacher, and spent his last years in Edessa, where he died in 373. He put the whole faith into hymns and taught choirs to sing them; the Syriac Churches call him the Harp of the Spirit. He wrote (in substance) that no one who drinks from the spring of God's word should be sad that he cannot drink it all; let him rejoice that it is inexhaustible. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church. The Kerala Churches of the Syriac tradition still sing his words.
outline: Ask: is there a rule you once obeyed only because you had to, and later came to love because you understood why?
Point 1 · A letter written on hearts
Our competence is from God, who makes us ministers of a new covenant.
Point 2 · The letter and the Spirit
The Law is holy; the Spirit writes it within us and gives life.
Point 3 · Not to abolish but to fulfill
Jesus brings the Law to its full meaning, as St Ephrem sang it.
“I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.”
live: Choose one commandment you keep only outwardly, and ask the Holy Spirit today to write it on your heart.
Following St Ephrem, sing or listen to one hymn today and let its words become your prayer.
2027-06-09.prayer: Holy God, you spoke to Moses in the cloud and gave your people the holy Law. Now through Jesus Christ you have made us ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of Spirit. Write your will on our hearts, so that we keep your commandments not from fear but from love. Lord Jesus, you came not to abolish but to fulfill; bring our lives to their full meaning in you. Through the prayers of St Ephrem, Harp of the Spirit, may our words and songs give you glory. Amen.
altar: Just before the consecration the priest stretches his hands over the bread and wine and asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they may become the Body and Blood of Christ. The Spirit who gives life is at work on the altar. St Ephrem loved to sing that in the bread there is fire and Spirit (in substance). After the consecration we pray that the same Spirit may gather us, who receive the Body and Blood of Christ, into one body, a letter of Christ written on human hearts.

quick: Paul says the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts; his competence as a minister comes from God.
The Law of Sinai came in glory and is holy, but the letter alone cannot give life; the Spirit writes God's will within us.
Jesus came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfill them; St Ephrem, the Harp of the Spirit, sang this faith in his hymns.
2027-06-09.action: Pray slowly through the Ten Commandments tonight, and thank Jesus for one that he has helped you to keep from the heart.
2027-06-09.question: Do I keep God's commandments only because I must, or because I have come to love them?
kidsaint: Ephrem lived about 1,700 years ago in a city called Nisibis, near the border of the Roman Empire. He was a deacon, which means a helper of the bishop. He loved God so much that he wrote hundreds of hymns, poems you can sing, about Jesus, Mary, the Bible and the sacraments. He taught choirs of women and girls to sing them in church, so that everybody could learn the faith by heart. People called him the Harp of the Holy Spirit. At the end of his life, when there was a famine, he worked hard to bring food to the hungry. Lesson: you can praise God with your voice and your songs, and you can help others learn about Jesus through music.

family.explain: Jesus said: I did not come to throw away God's commandments, but to fulfill them, to show their full meaning. God's commandments are like a fence that keeps us safe. Jesus teaches us to keep them not because we are afraid, but because we love God and love our neighbours. The Holy Spirit writes God's law in our hearts.
family.intention: We pray for all who teach the faith: parents, catechists and Sunday-school teachers, and for church choirs.
family.ask: Ask: “Which of the Ten Commandments is hardest for our family? How can we help one another keep it with love?”

illus: A catechism teacher in a parish near Kollam found her Class Six students bored by the Ten Commandments. One Sunday she brought a mango sapling tied to a stick. She said: this stick is like the Law; it keeps the young tree straight while it is weak. But the life is not in the stick; the life is in the sap that rises from the roots. The Holy Spirit is the sap. When the tree is grown strong, it stands straight by itself, but it has not thrown away what the stick taught it. A boy said: so Jesus did not throw away the stick; he gave the tree its life. She said that was the best summary of Matthew 5:17 she had ever heard. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Holy Spirit, Lord and giver of life, write God's law on our hearts. Make us letters of Christ that all can read. Amen.
share: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts (2 Corinthians 3:2). If people read my life as a letter of Christ, what would they read?
The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). Is my faith a matter of outward rules only, or is it alive in the Spirit?
I have come not to abolish but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17). How does Jesus show me the full meaning of a commandment I find hard?
pm.resp: Holy is the Lord our God.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a minister of the new covenant, full of the Spirit who gives life.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may grow in love of his name and in faithfulness to his covenant.
For all who teach and sing the faith, through the prayers of St Ephrem, especially catechists and church choirs.
For the Syriac Churches of Kerala and the Middle East, who honour Mar Aprem, and for Christians in the lands where he lived.
For our group, that the Spirit may write the commandments of God on our hearts.
pm.close: God of the covenant, you gave your Law in glory and your Spirit in greater glory. Make us faithful in the smallest things and generous in the greatest. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, some preachers in Corinth carried impressive letters of recommendation, and they asked: where are Paul's letters? Paul answers: you are my letter. You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts (2 Corinthians 3:2), written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. The best proof of a minister's work is not a certificate but a changed life.

Then Paul says: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). He does not mean that God's Law is bad. Paul loved the Law. He means that a law written only on stone, outside us, can tell us what is right, but it cannot give us the strength to do it. When we fail, it can only condemn us. The Holy Spirit writes God's will inside us, in our hearts, and gives us the power to live it. That is the new covenant God promised through the prophet Jeremiah.

But the Gospel warns us not to go to the other extreme. Jesus says: do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17). The commandments are not thrown away. Jesus shows their full meaning and gives us his Spirit to keep them with love. A child obeys his mother first because he must, and later because he loves her. That is the journey from letter to Spirit.

Today the Church remembers St Ephrem, a deacon of the fourth century, whom our Syriac sister Churches in Kerala call Mar Aprem. He turned the faith into songs and taught people to sing it. He is called the Harp of the Holy Spirit. Let us ask him to help us sing God's commandments in our hearts, and to become letters of Christ that our families and neighbours can read. Amen.
kids: Children, imagine your mother writes on a paper: brush your teeth, say your prayers, help your little brother. You can obey the paper because you have to. But Jesus wants something better: he wants the Holy Spirit to write God's rules inside your heart, so that you do good because you love God. Jesus said: I did not come to throw away God's commandments, but to fulfill them. Today we remember St Ephrem, who wrote beautiful songs about Jesus. Sing a hymn to Jesus today!

intro: A letter written on hearts, the holy Law fulfilled and not abolished, and the Spirit who makes us keep it with love.

sub: Not with ink but with the Spirit.
q: Now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to speak.
Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God,
points.apply: Before any task of service this week, pray: Lord, my competence is from you.

sub: Stone tablets and hearts of flesh.
q: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.
points.apply: Choose one commandment you find hard and pray each day this week for the Spirit to write it on your heart.

points.h: Not to abolish but to fulfill
sub: Not one stroke of a letter.
The Harp of the Spirit sings it.
q: The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the decrees of the Lord are sure, making wise the simple;

Therefore, whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do the same, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
points.apply: Teach one child, by word or example, one of God's commandments this week.

concl: Paul's ministry is the work of the Spirit, who writes God's holy Law on human hearts and gives life.
Jesus fulfils the Law and the prophets; St Ephrem teaches us to sing that fulfilment with our whole life.
2027-06-09.resolve: Each day this week, keep one commandment from the heart, and thank the Spirit who makes it possible.
